title: Riding home
hookLine: picture six: riding the ox home, playing a flute (Ox-Herding 6)
tomorrow: the herder gets home. so where did the ox go?

cards: Some drives home after a hard thing are silent. On others, the music goes up and somebody sings badly. Kuoan's sixth picture is the second kind.
The herder sits on the ox's back, heading home, playing a flute. Why music, right here? The preface answers plainly: the struggle is over.

teach.h: A CHILDREN'S TUNE, EYES ON CLOUDS.
teach.b: Gain and loss don't touch him now. He hums a woodcutter's song, plays a village children's tune, and looks up at the clouds. If someone calls him back, he won't turn around.

Look at what's changed since picture four. Then, the herder hauled on the rope with all his strength while the ox bolted for the mountains. Now the same ox carries him home, and his hands are free for music.
The verse: riding the ox, he heads home at ease; the flute's sound drifts into the evening haze; every beat holds more than words, and whoever knows the tune needs no explaining.
That's Zen's teaching at this stage: long practice ripens into ease, and the ease is musical, not grim. A neighbor tradition has a flute too. Rumi's Masnavi opens with a reed.
In Whinfield's translation: "Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains," grieving that it was cut from its reed bed. Sufi tradition reads that reed as the soul longing to return to God.
What they share: the truest thing about the way gets said by a flute, not an argument.

teach.h: RUMI'S REED: A SONG OF LONGING.
teach.b: An honest difference: Rumi's reed sings because it's far from home, a song of separation and longing for the Beloved.

teach.h: KUOAN'S FLUTE: A SONG OF HOME.
teach.b: Kuoan's herder plays because he's nearly home, and he names no God at all.
Longing and arriving: two songs, both played on breath.

how: Zen students read the sixth ox-herding picture as practice ripening into ease; Sufis hear the reed of Rumi's Masnavi as the soul's longing for God, and the ney flute is played in Sufi gatherings. People on this path let joy and music belong to practice.

games.q: a friend says real spiritual music has to be solemn; a happy tune is just entertainment. what does picture six offer her?
o: the herder plays a village children's tune; at this stage of the way, joy is music too.
she's right: only solemn sacred music belongs anywhere near the way.
music doesn't matter at all; Zen leaves no room for any kind of song.
games.why: in Kuoan's sixth picture, the herder hums a woodcutter's song and plays a children's tune, and whoever knows the tune needs no words.

practice: Hum or play something simple for the two minutes, any tune you know, even one note at a time. Let it be the herder's song: no performance, nobody to impress, just the sound of going home.
